stem:
Element **X** is in Period 4 of the Periodic Table. It forms two common ions, X²⁺ and X³⁺. The X³⁺ ion has the electron configuration [Ar] 3d⁵. X²⁺ and X³⁺ ions catalyse the reaction between peroxodisulfate ions and iodide ions:

$\ce{S2O8^2- + 2I- -> 2SO4^2- + I2}$

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Identify element **X** (name or symbol).
parts.explanation: Fe: [Ar] 3d⁶4s²; Fe³⁺ loses the 4s electrons and one 3d electron: [Ar] 3d⁵.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Complete the electron configurations.
parts.explanation: 4s electrons are lost first: Fe [Ar] 3d⁶4s², Fe²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁶.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Why is zinc not classed as a transition element?

options.content: Its only ion, Zn²⁺, has a full 3d sub-shell.
options.rationale: Correct: Zn²⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰.

options.content: It has no electrons in the 3d sub-shell.
options.rationale: Zinc has ten 3d electrons.

options.content: It does not form any positive ions.
options.rationale: Zinc forms Zn²⁺.

options.content: It is in the s-block of the Periodic Table.
options.rationale: Zinc is in the d-block.

parts.explanation: A transition element forms at least one stable ion with an incomplete d sub-shell.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why transition elements show variable oxidation states.

points.description: The 3d and 4s sub-shells are close in energy
So different numbers of electrons (4s and 3d) can be lost or used in bonding with similar energy input, giving several stable states

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The 3d and 4s electrons have similar energies, so a variable number of them can be removed or used in bonding without a large jump in ionisation energy, giving several stable oxidation states.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Give the highest oxidation state shown by manganese in its compounds.
parts.explanation: +7 (in MnO₄⁻): all seven 4s and 3d electrons are used.
parts.workedSolution: 1. +7 (in MnO₄⁻): all seven 4s and 3d electrons are used.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain, with two equations, how Fe²⁺ ions catalyse the reaction between peroxodisulfate and iodide ions, and why the uncatalysed reaction is slow.

points.description: $\ce{2Fe^3+ + 2I- -> 2Fe^2+ + I2}$ (Fe²⁺ regenerated)
Uncatalysed: two negative ions repel, so the activation energy is high; each catalysed step is between oppositely charged ions (lower activation energy)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: S₂O₈²⁻ + 2Fe²⁺ → 2SO₄²⁻ + 2Fe³⁺, then 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂, so the iron(II) is regenerated. The uncatalysed reaction is between two negative ions, which repel, giving a high activation energy; in each catalysed step the ions have opposite charges, so the activation energy is lower. This works because iron can change between the +2 and +3 states.

explanation: X = Fe; variable oxidation states arise from close 3d and 4s energies; Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ catalysis by two steps between oppositely charged ions.
hints: Transition metal atoms lose 4s electrons before 3d electrons.
A homogeneous catalyst must be regenerated.

stem:
Tendai carried out these reactions starting from aqueous copper(II) sulfate, which contains $\ce{[Cu(H2O)6]^2+}$.

| step | reagent | observation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | aqueous ammonia, a few drops | pale blue precipitate |
| 2 | aqueous ammonia, in excess | precipitate dissolves; deep blue solution |
| 3 | concentrated hydrochloric acid added to fresh copper(II) sulfate | yellow-green solution |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What is the shape of the copper complex formed in step 3?

options.rationale: Correct: [CuCl₄]²⁻, four large chloride ligands.
Six chloride ions do not fit round Cu²⁺.
Linear complexes have two ligands, e.g. [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺.
Three-coordinate complexes are not formed here.

parts.explanation: [CuCl₄]²⁻ is tetrahedral (coordination number 4).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Give the formula of the deep blue complex ion in step 2. (Type it as, for example, [Ni(NH3)6]2+.)
parts.explanation: Partial substitution: four NH₃ replace four H₂O.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Write equations for steps 1 and 2.

points.description: Step 1: $\ce{[Cu(H2O)6]^2+ + 2NH3 -> Cu(OH)2(H2O)4 + 2NH4+}$ (or with 2OH⁻ forming Cu(OH)₂)
Step 2: $\ce{Cu(OH)2(H2O)4 + 4NH3 -> [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]^2+ + 2OH- + 2H2O}$ (or from the aqua ion: $\ce{[Cu(H2O)6]^2+ + 4NH3 -> [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]^2+ + 4H2O}$)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Step 1: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 2NH₃ → Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄ + 2NH₄⁺. Step 2: Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 2OH⁻ + 2H₂O.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why copper(II) complexes are coloured and why the colour changes in step 2.

points.description: Ligands split the 3d orbitals into two groups of different energy (ΔE)
An electron is promoted from a lower to a higher d orbital by absorbing visible light of frequency matching ΔE; the complementary colour is seen
Ammonia ligands give a different (larger) ΔE than water, so a different wavelength is absorbed and the colour changes

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In a complex the ligands split the five 3d orbitals into lower- and higher-energy sets separated by ΔE. Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) has a partly filled d sub-shell, so an electron can be promoted by absorbing visible light whose frequency corresponds to ΔE (ΔE = hf); the colour seen is the complementary colour. Ammonia ligands split the d orbitals by a different, larger amount than water, so a different frequency is absorbed and the colour changes from pale blue to deep blue.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Complete the statements about the deep blue complex.

payload.template: Coordination number of copper: {{blank:a}}. Overall charge on the complex ion: {{blank:b}}.

parts.explanation: Four NH₃ and two H₂O: six dative bonds; neutral ligands, so the charge is that of Cu²⁺.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: In the deep blue complex, the energy gap ΔE between the split d orbitals is larger than in [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺.
parts.explanation: True: ammonia splits the d orbitals more, so light of higher frequency is absorbed.

explanation: Cu(OH)₂ precipitate, then ligand exchange to [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺; [CuCl₄]²⁻ is tetrahedral; colour from d-d transitions whose ΔE depends on the ligand.
hints: Ammonia acts first as a base, then as a ligand.
Colour: absorbed frequency is linked to ΔE.

stem:
This question is about isomerism in complexes of platinum(II) and nickel(II). 1,2-diaminoethane, H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂, is abbreviated to *en*.

| complex | geometry |
|---|---|
| [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] | square planar |
| [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ | octahedral |
| [Ni(en)₂(H₂O)₂]²⁺ | octahedral |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the type of ligand that *en* is, in terms of the number of dative bonds it forms.
parts.explanation: Each en forms two dative bonds, one from each nitrogen lone pair.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: What type of stereoisomerism does [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] show?

options.rationale: A square planar complex has a plane of symmetry, so it is not chiral.
Neither isomer is chiral.
The isomers differ in spatial arrangement, not in connectivity.
Correct: square planar with two pairs of identical ligands.

parts.explanation: Cis (the anticancer drug cisplatin) and trans isomers.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Describe the two isomers of [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] in words and state which one is polar.

points.description: Cis: the two Cl ligands are next to each other (90°); trans: the two Cl ligands are opposite each other (180°)
The cis isomer is polar (dipoles do not cancel); the trans isomer is non-polar (dipoles cancel)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In the cis isomer the two chloride ligands are adjacent, at 90° to each other; in the trans isomer they are opposite, at 180°. The cis isomer has an overall dipole and is polar; in the trans isomer the bond dipoles cancel, so it is non-polar.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Which of the complexes in the table exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images?

options.rationale: Square planar complexes have a plane of symmetry.
Correct: three bidentate ligands make a chiral propeller shape.
The trans isomer has a plane of symmetry.
Six identical monodentate ligands: no isomers.

parts.explanation: [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ is chiral.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: How many stereoisomers does [Ni(en)₂(H₂O)₂]²⁺ have in total?
parts.explanation: Trans (one, achiral) and cis (a pair of optical isomers): 3.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Trans (one, achiral) and cis (a pair of optical isomers): 3.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain why [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ shows optical isomerism and how the two isomers could be distinguished.

points.description: The complex has no plane of symmetry, so it and its mirror image are non-superimposable (chiral)
The two enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light by equal amounts in opposite directions

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The three bidentate en ligands are arranged like a propeller with no plane of symmetry, so the complex is chiral: its mirror image cannot be superimposed on it. The two optical isomers rotate the plane of plane-polarised light by the same angle in opposite directions.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Cisplatin works as an anticancer drug because it binds to DNA, preventing cancer cells from dividing.
parts.explanation: True: after ligand exchange of Cl⁻, platinum binds to nitrogen atoms of guanine bases.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Give the Cl–Pt–Cl bond angle, in degrees, in the trans isomer of [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂].
parts.explanation: Opposite corners of the square: 180°.

explanation: en is bidentate; [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] has cis/trans isomers (cis polar); [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ is chiral; [Ni(en)₂(H₂O)₂]²⁺ has three stereoisomers.
hints: Look for a plane of symmetry.

stem:
Stability constants of some copper(II) complexes at 298 K (data: textbook values).

| complex | Kstab |
|---|---|
| [CuCl₄]²⁻ | 4.2 × 10⁵ mol⁻⁴ dm¹² |
| [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ | 1.2 × 10¹³ mol⁻⁴ dm¹² |
| [Cu(EDTA)]²⁻ | 6.3 × 10¹⁸ mol⁻¹ dm³ |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Define the stability constant, Kstab, of a complex ion.

points.description: The equilibrium constant for the formation of the complex ion from its constituent (aqua) metal ion and ligands in a solvent

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Kstab is the equilibrium constant for the formation of a complex ion in a solvent from its constituent ions or molecules.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which is the expression for Kstab of [CuCl₄]²⁻?

options.rationale: This is the inverse (the instability constant).
The chloride term must be raised to the power 4.
Correct: products over reactants, water omitted.
Water, the solvent, is not included.

parts.explanation: Kstab = [CuCl₄²⁻]/([Cu²⁺][Cl⁻]⁴).

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: In a solution at equilibrium, [CuCl₄²⁻] = 0.0400 mol dm⁻³ and [Cl⁻] = 5.00 mol dm⁻³. Calculate [Cu²⁺(aq)], in mol dm⁻³, to three significant figures.
parts.explanation: [Cu²⁺] = 0.0400 ÷ (4.2 × 10⁵ × 5.00⁴) = 0.0400 ÷ 2.63 × 10⁸ = 1.52 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³. Forgetting the power of 4 gives 1.90 × 10⁻⁸.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Which list shows the complexes in order of increasing stability?

options.rationale: This is decreasing stability.
Correct: larger Kstab means a more stable complex.
Kstab for the chloro complex is the smallest.
EDTA has by far the largest Kstab.

parts.explanation: 4.2 × 10⁵ < 1.2 × 10¹³ < 6.3 × 10¹⁸ (comparing complexes of the same metal).

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Aqueous EDTA⁴⁻ is added to the deep blue solution of [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺. Predict what happens and explain the chelate effect.

points.description: EDTA replaces the ammonia and water ligands (ligand exchange) because [Cu(EDTA)]²⁻ has a much larger Kstab; the deep blue colour fades to a paler blue
One hexadentate EDTA⁴⁻ releases six ligand molecules, so the number of particles increases and ΔS is positive, favouring the chelate

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: EDTA⁴⁻ displaces the ammonia and water ligands because its complex is far more stable (Kstab 6.3 × 10¹⁸), and the deep blue colour becomes paler. One EDTA⁴⁻ ion replaces six monodentate ligands: [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + EDTA⁴⁻ → [Cu(EDTA)]²⁻ + 4NH₃ + 2H₂O, so the number of particles rises, the entropy change is positive, and the chelate complex is favoured.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Calculate lg Kstab (log₁₀ Kstab) for [Cu(EDTA)]²⁻, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Adding concentrated hydrochloric acid to [Cu(EDTA)]²⁻ would readily convert it into [CuCl₄]²⁻.
parts.explanation: False: Kstab for the EDTA complex is about 10¹³ times larger, so chloride cannot displace EDTA significantly.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: How many dative bonds does one EDTA⁴⁻ ion form to the copper(II) ion?
parts.explanation: EDTA⁴⁻ is hexadentate: two N and four O donor atoms.
parts.workedSolution: 1. EDTA⁴⁻ is hexadentate: two N and four O donor atoms.

explanation: [Cu²⁺] = 1.52 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³; stability Cl⁻ < NH₃ < EDTA; EDTA wins by the chelate (entropy) effect.
hints: A larger Kstab means a more stable complex.

stem: Nyasha standardised a solution of iron(II) ammonium sulfate. 25.0 cm³ portions, acidified with dilute sulfuric acid, needed a mean titre of 23.40 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ potassium manganate(VII). Data (E⦵ / V): MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ ⇌ Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O +1.52; Fe³⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺ +0.77; O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ ⇌ 2H₂O +1.23.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Construct the ionic equation for the titration reaction.

points.description: Correct species: MnO₄⁻, H⁺ and Fe²⁺ forming Mn²⁺, Fe³⁺ and H₂O
Balanced: $\ce{MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe^2+ -> Mn^2+ + 5Fe^3+ + 4H2O}$

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O (charge +17 on each side).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the concentration of iron(II), in mol dm⁻³, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate E⦵cell, in V, for the titration reaction, to two decimal places.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: What is the colour change at the end-point?

options.rationale: That happens to each drop before the end-point.
That is dichromate(VI).
That is an iodine-starch end-point.
Correct: the first excess of MnO₄⁻.

parts.explanation: Manganate(VII) is self-indicating.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Use the data to explain why iron(II) solutions must be freshly prepared or standardised just before use.

points.description: E⦵cell for oxidation of Fe²⁺ by oxygen = 1.23 − 0.77 = +0.46 V, so it is feasible
Dissolved oxygen slowly oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ (4Fe²⁺ + O₂ + 4H⁺ → 4Fe³⁺ + 2H₂O), so the Fe²⁺ concentration falls with time

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: For 4Fe²⁺ + O₂ + 4H⁺ → 4Fe³⁺ + 2H₂O, E⦵cell = 1.23 − 0.77 = +0.46 V, so air oxidises iron(II). The reaction is slow, but the iron(II) concentration falls on standing, so the solution must be made fresh or standardised just before use.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Name a reagent that gives a deep red colour if the iron(II) solution contains some iron(III).
parts.explanation: Thiocyanate gives deep red [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅]²⁺.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Hydrochloric acid would be a suitable acid for this titration.
parts.explanation: False: MnO₄⁻ would oxidise Cl⁻ to Cl₂ (E⦵cell = 1.52 − 1.36 = +0.16 V), giving a high titre.

explanation: [Fe²⁺] = 0.0936 mol dm⁻³; E⦵cell = +0.75 V; air oxidises Fe²⁺ (+0.46 V).
hints: One MnO₄⁻ reacts with five Fe²⁺.
Compare E⦵ for O₂/H₂O and Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺.

stem: This question is about copper and nickel. Data (E⦵ / V): Cu⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Cu +0.52; Cu²⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Cu⁺ +0.15. (Ar Cu = 63.5; F = 9.65 × 10⁴ C mol⁻¹)

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate E⦵cell, in V, for 2Cu⁺(aq) → Cu(s) + Cu²⁺(aq), to two decimal places.
parts.explanation: 0.52 − 0.15 = +0.37 V: copper(I) disproportionates.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Copper(I) oxide is warmed with dilute sulfuric acid. State what is seen and write the equation.

points.description: A pink-brown solid (copper) and a blue solution (copper(II) sulfate) form
$\ce{Cu2O + H2SO4 -> Cu + CuSO4 + H2O}$

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A pink-brown deposit of copper forms in a blue solution: Cu₂O + H₂SO₄ → Cu + CuSO₄ + H₂O.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Why is copper(I) iodide stable even though Cu⁺(aq) disproportionates?

options.content: Iodide ions oxidise copper(I) to copper(II).
options.rationale: Iodide is a reducing agent, not an oxidising agent here.

options.content: Copper(I) iodide has a partly filled d sub-shell.
options.rationale: Cu⁺ is d¹⁰.

options.content: It is insoluble, so very little free Cu⁺(aq) is present.
options.rationale: Correct: precipitation removes Cu⁺ from solution.

options.content: The iodide ion is a bidentate ligand.
options.rationale: Iodide is monodentate; the key is insolubility.

parts.explanation: Insoluble CuI keeps [Cu⁺(aq)] tiny, so disproportionation cannot occur.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: In the electrolytic purification of copper, a current of 4.00 A flows for 2.00 hours. Calculate the mass of copper deposited, in g, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Give two uses of nickel and the property each depends on.

points.description: Hydrogenation catalyst for making margarine (adsorbs H₂ and C=C compounds on its surface)
Stainless steel / cupronickel coins / alnico magnets (corrosion resistance, hardness or magnetism)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Finely divided nickel catalyses the hydrogenation of vegetable oils to margarine because reactants adsorb on its surface; nickel is alloyed in stainless steel, which resists corrosion.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Name the alloy of copper and tin.
parts.explanation: Bronze (brass is copper and zinc).

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: In the electrolytic purification of copper, gold impurities collect in the anode slime.
parts.explanation: True: gold is not oxidised at the anode.

explanation: Disproportionation +0.37 V; 9.48 g of copper deposited.
hints: Cu⁺ is both reduced and oxidised.
